title: Purchasing playbook — dedicated throughput, SLAs & isolation
content:
TL;DR:
A concise purchasing playbook to help AE/SE/procurement land Dedicated capacity deals with clear SLA commitments (uptime + P99 latency + throughput floors), contractual isolation terms (network, data handling, KMS), and commercial constructs that procurement expects (committed spend, burst credits, conversion clause).

Audience:
- Account Executives and Solutions Engineers preparing procurement decks
- Sales engineering leads drafting SOWs
- Legal and Revenue Ops who review SLA/terms

Key objectives:
1) Remove ambiguity for procurement teams by providing concrete, measurable commitments.
2) Provide defensible technical language around isolation and data controls.
3) Offer commercial options that accelerate signings while protecting Redwood’s capacity economics.

Procurement checklist (recommended order of play):
- Intro one-pager: short bullets on what Dedicated includes (reserved GPU pool, isolated tenant, private control plane option).
- Capacity profile: expected throughput (tokens/sec per GPU), example RPS to slots mapping, expected concurrency.
- SLA summary: uptime target, availability credits, P99 latency target for typical prompt sizes, maintenance window policy.
- Security/compliance: SOC2 report, KMS integration, VPC peering details, audit and logging retention options.
- Commercial: commit tiers, burst buffer rules, overage pricing, conversion rights to Private.
- SOW draft & timelines: onboarding milestones, acceptance tests, scale ramp schedule.
- Operational contact list and escalation matrix.

Recommended SLA language (working draft for legal):
- Availability: Redwood will provide Dedicated Capacity with Monthly Uptime Percentage of at least 99.95% measured at the tenant-level, excluding scheduled maintenance with >=72h notice.
- Throughput floor: For contracted capacity X GPUs, Redwood guarantees baseline sustained throughput equivalent to Y tokens/sec (example: 40 tokens/sec per A100-80GB-equivalent GPU) under typical workload assumptions (median prompt length 32 tokens).
- Latency SLO: 95% of single-request generations with prompt length <=64 tokens will complete within 1200ms; P99 latency target will be specified per-commit tier and measured under normal operating conditions.
- Credits: Availability or SLO misses result in service credits applied to monthly invoice according to a simple sliding scale (detailed percentages in SOW).
- Fallbacks: If Dedicated capacity is temporarily unavailable, Redwood will route traffic to pre-agreed compatible model variants under the customer’s policy; this behavior and pricing is explicitly stated in the SOW.

Notes on throughput guarantees (how to talk about it to customers):
- Be concrete: map GPU counts to request-per-minute examples for common prompt sizes (short chats, long completions, batch embeddings).
- Clarify assumptions: prefix caching usage, KV cache behavior, and whether streaming is included in the baseline.
- Offer two modes: "Committed throughput" (measured, SLA-backed) and "Burst pool" (best-effort, chargeable above committed usage).

Isolation & compliance language (talking points and redlines):
- Network: Dedicated tenants can be deployed into customer VPC (Private) or in logically isolated subnets with dedicated NAT & egress policies for Hosted Dedicated.
- Data handling: Customer data is logically segregated; we retain logs for X days (configurable). Include optional retention and deletion SLAs for regulated customers.
- Key management: Offer customer-managed KMS for model artifacts and request payloads where required.
- Auditability: Provide access to operational logs and an audit package; add SOC2 + ISO evidence references in SOW.

Commercial constructs (practical options that close deals):
- Commit tiers: 3-6-12 month buckets with step discounts (example: 10% for 6mo, 18% for 12mo).
- Burst credits: Pre-purchased burst credits amortized monthly to handle seasonal spikes.
- Conversion clause: Allow unused committed capacity to convert to Private deployment credits within 90 days of purchase (reduces friction for customers evaluating air-gapped needs).
- Ramp clauses: Lower initial commit for fast POC (1–3 months) with a defined ramp schedule to full committed capacity.
- Early termination: Simple exit with pro-rated refunds after minimum commitment, but with defined settlement for reserved hardware scheduling.

Competitive positioning (how to differentiate vs hyperscalers and self-hosted vendors):
- Vs hyperscalers: Sell predictable economics + simpler dev UX. Hyperscalers sell raw capacity but not inference-optimized runtime; Redwood provides inference-level unit economics, model-aware routing, and built-in fallback behaviors. Emphasize observability and token-level billing granularity that maps to developer metrics.
- Vs inference runtimes/self-hosted solutions: Sell reduced ops burden — we run updates, manage kernel selections, deliver SLAs, and provide a single support path. For customers who want full control, highlight Redwood Private as a migration path with the same API surface.
- Example positioning line: "Dedicated from Redwood gives you the predictability of reserved capacity with inference-grade SLOs and the operational guardrails of a managed service — without owning the full stack."

Procurement objections & scripted responses (sales enablement):
- Objection: "We can just run on cloud instances ourselves cheaper."
  Response: "Upfront GPU cost is only part of the TCO — our runtime reduces token cost with batching, caching, and optimized kernels; we also eliminate dev+ops time. We can run a 6-week TCO comparison for your workload."
- Objection: "We need strict isolation / air-gap."
  Response: "We offer Private (VPC + on-prem options) and customer-managed KMS. We can add contractual language and a short technical appendix for your auditors."
- Objection: "How do we measure SLA misses?"
  Response: "We provide per-tenant telemetry and a clear SLO measurement spec. We’ll include a sample measurement report during onboarding and quarterly review."

Procurement-ready collateral (what to attach to RFP/RFI):
- One-page summary of Dedicated feature set and SLAs.
- SOW template with onboarding milestones and acceptance tests.
- Security package: SOC2, pen test summary, data handling appendix.
- Example capacity profile & throughput calculator spreadsheet (attach).
- Case study blurb + reference contact (if allowed).

Operational readiness & onboarding milestones (recommended SOW):
1) Kickoff & environment design (2 weeks) — network, IAM, KMS decisions.
2) Provisioning (1–2 weeks) — reserved pools, alerting, SLO wiring.
3) Acceptance tests (1 week) — run synthetic load tests for throughput/latency verification.
4) Cutover & hypercare (2–4 weeks) — real traffic ramp with SE support.
5) Quarterly review & SLO tuning.

Open questions / items for legal/engineering to finalize:
- Exact measurable definition for "throughput floor" for different GPU classes (need infra input).
- Maintenance window maximum allowed per quarter before SLA adjustments.
- Template for burst-to-committed conversion pricing.
- Standard wording for audit access to logs (scope & retention).

Appendix: Suggested collateral filenames to include with deal packet:
- "Redwood Dedicated one-pager (procurement)"
- "SOW-template-dedicated-capacity.docx"
- "Throughput-calculator-example.xlsx"

Next steps (owner: Ava Martinez):
- Finalize numeric throughput assumptions with infra (owner: Jonah Kim) by 2025-03-12.
- Draft SOW clause for credits and maintenance with legal (owner: Priya Desai) by 2025-03-19.
- Build a standard one-pager and a short sales script for AE/SEs and publish to enablement space.

Internal notes (rough):
- Keep language modular so we can swap different GPU-class throughput numbers per region.
- Consider adding a short technical appendix showing how caching and batching produce real cost savings vs unmanaged instances — strong win in procurement conversations.
